sections.title: What a professional tutor invoice must show
sections.body: A tutoring invoice needs to be specific enough that parents or adult learners never question what they are paying for. Always include the student's name, especially if the parent is the client paying the bill. List the date and exact duration of every session. If you provide textbooks, revision guides, or past papers, list these materials as separate line items rather than hiding them in your hourly rate. Finally, your invoice must clearly state your cancellation policy. Having your no-show rules written on the document protects you if a student forgets to log on or cancels at the last minute.

sections.title: How tutor work is priced and billed
sections.body: Tutors generally bill in three ways: pay-as-you-go sessions, group classes, or prepaid blocks. Pay-as-you-go is simple but leaves you vulnerable to cancellations. Group classes require a different rate structure, which your invoice should clearly reflect. Many full-time tutors prefer selling prepaid blocks of lessons. When a client buys a block of ten sessions, you invoice for the total upfront. In accounting terms, this prepaid block is unearned income until you actually teach the classes. You can use our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator to create these upfront bills easily, keeping your cash flow healthy while you work through the block.

sections.title: Managing terms, deposits, and chasing payments
sections.body: Chasing parents for money is the worst part of tutoring. To prevent late payments, set strict payment terms. For pay-as-you-go lessons, request payment within 24 hours of the session. For prepaid blocks, require full payment before the first lesson begins. If you are preparing a student for a major exam over several months, you might take a deposit to secure their regular weekly slot. When payments are late, send a polite but firm payment reminder. Keep a clear ledger of who has paid and who has not, so you never accidentally teach a third lesson when the first two remain unpaid.

faqs.q: How do I invoice for a prepaid block of lessons?
faqs.a: Create a single invoice for the total cost of the block before the first session begins. Describe the item clearly, such as a block of ten mathematics sessions. Once paid, you treat this as unearned income and deduct one session from their balance each week. This secures your income and reduces the administrative work of billing every single week.

faqs.q: Where should I put my cancellation policy on the invoice?
faqs.a: Add your cancellation and no-show policy to the notes or terms section at the bottom of the invoice. Keep it brief and clear. For example, state that sessions cancelled with less than 24 hours of notice will be billed at the full rate. Having this in writing on every financial document prevents arguments if a student fails to attend.

faqs.q: Should I bill parents or the student directly?
faqs.a: For school-age children, the parent or guardian is your client. Address the invoice to the parent, but include the student's name in the line item description so the parent knows exactly which child the bill relates to. For adult learners and university students, you address the invoice directly to the student.

faqs.q: How do I charge for textbooks and revision materials?
faqs.a: Never hide the cost of physical materials inside your hourly teaching rate. Instead, add a separate line item to your invoice for the specific textbook, past paper pack, or revision guide you provided. This keeps your hourly rate transparent and shows the client exactly what physical goods they are purchasing from you alongside your time.
